It's an oddity, this, but worth seeing for him.
While the two lead performances compel, its glaring deficit is that it strains too hard to jazz things up experimentally.
The first half is pulled down by the weight of its laboured reinvention.

“If you inspect the plot too closely, it seems faintly absurd,” the estimable Benedict Nightingale wrote when he saw Suchet give what was, by all accounts, a masterful performance back in 2005. Here, that fine actor Ben Daniels is required to play the villain as a shrill, camp figure — think Rudolf Nureyev channelling Professor Moriarty.

rv.q: It is a rare thing to see a revival of Man and Boy. Last performed in London in 2005, with David Suchet as the Romanian billionaire Gregor Antonescu, it remains one of Terence Rattigan’s largely forgotten works, while others, such as The Deep Blue Sea, shine as classics.

Most critics praise Lau for taking a bold approach to dusty and unloved Rattigan play, but for some, the arch inventiveness goes too far, getting in the way of a story about corruption that could speak to us more sincerely and directly.
With the peerless Ben Daniels outstanding as Antonescu, it has a savagery and sharpness that make it utterly compelling.
The strange carapace works for the seedy and sinister first half, but when the small stuff takes over the domesticity just rattles weakly inside the vast shell Lau has created.
These witty touches are refreshing – but they feel like a bit of a mismatch with Rattigan's serious portrait of moral corruption, which offers more to respect than to enjoy.
Rattigan's MAN AND BOY isn't considered among his finest plays.
I’d venture that the play itself feels a little better than its bad rep would suggest – unlikely and ultimately undercooked, yes, but nonetheless hugely entertaining and provocative.
